extracted.intended_audience: translators of classical Greek (especially Aeschylus) and informed readers comparing translations
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for producing an English translation of Aeschylus' Agamemnon emphasizing fidelity to the Greek text, conservative editorial treatment, and specific transliteration/spelling practices. Intended as a translator's stylistic and editorial rubric rather than a literary modernization.

rubrics_metrics.name: Literalness except when violently un-English
rubrics_metrics.description: I should require him to be literal at every cost save that of absolute violence to our language.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aim for a 'very literal' rendering of each phrase ('furnish me with the very turn of each phrase in as Greek a fashion as English will bear'). Be literal even at the expense of sonority or elegance, only relaxing literalness when the literal reading would produce incoherent or violently unnatural English.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tolerance for archaic/allowable constructions
rubrics_metrics.description: The use of certain allowable constructions which, happening to be out of daily favour, are all the more appropriate to archaic workmanship, is no violence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use English constructions that may seem archaic or unfashionable if they better reflect the archaic character of the original Greek; such choices are acceptable to preserve tone and texture.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reject amplifications and embellishments
rubrics_metrics.description: With respect to amplifications and embellishments,--anything rather than, with the good farmer, experience that most signal of mortifications, 'to gape for Aeschylus and get Theognis.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid adding explanatory material, expansions, or stylistic 'brightening' that substitute another author's diction or change the original character. Better an austere, faithful version than an embellished, misleading one.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preserve repetition; avoid gratuitous synonym-substitution
rubrics_metrics.description: I should especially decline ... the employment of a new word for some old one,--πόνος, or μέγας, or τέλος, ... recurring four times in three lines: for though such substitution may be in itself perfectly justifiable, yet this exercise of ingenuity ought to be within the competence of the unaided English reader if he likes to show himself ingenious.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When the Greek repeats words, the translator should generally retain corresponding repetition rather than replace repeated terms with different English synonyms to show variety; such 'variety' can mask the original's rhetorical effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accept difficulty/obscurity rather than over-smoothing
rubrics_metrics.description: I should expect the result to prove very hard reading indeed if it were meant to resemble Aeschylus, 'ξυμβαλεῖν οὐ ῥᾴδιος' ('not easy to understand').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not excessively smooth or simplify genuinely obscure, ambiguous, or dense passages to make them easy; preserve intended difficulty and ambiguity where they are features of the original.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conservative treatment of corrupt or interpolated text
rubrics_metrics.description: The text is sadly corrupt, probably interpolated, and certainly mutilated; and no unlearned person enjoys the scholar's privilege of trying his fancy upon each obstacle whenever he comes to a stoppage, and effectually clearing the way by suppressing what seems to lie in it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid guessing, suppressing, or freely altering passages judged corrupt unless supported by strong scholarly evidence; do not casually emend the text to 'clear the way' for smoother English.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer earlier readings unless recent criticism is compelling
rubrics_metrics.description: Following no editor exclusively, I keep to the earlier readings so long as sense can be made out of them, but disregard, I hope, little of importance in recent criticism so far as I have fallen in with it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use earlier/manuscript readings as the default when they yield sense; consider recent editorial suggestions only when they clearly improve sense or are important scholarship—avoid wholesale adoption of modern conjectures without cause.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fidelity over sonority or poetic polish
rubrics_metrics.description: The poorest translation, provided only it be faithful,--though it reproduce all the artistic confusion of tenses, moods, and persons, with which the original teems,--will not only suffice to display ... 'the action of the piece'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prioritize faithfulness to meaning, structure, and dramatic action even if that preserves awkward tenses, moods, or lack of smooth poetic polish. Convey the poem's ideas and action faithfully rather than seeking superior English musicality at the cost of accuracy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conservative non-beautification of the original
rubrics_metrics.description: I have left eyes and mouths everywhere as I found them, and this conservatism is all that claims praise ...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not 'beautify' or 'improve' the author's words for the sake of English aesthetics (analogous to Old Muytens' harmful 'beautifying' of a painting). Retain original roughnesses, peculiarities, and defects unless there is clear reason to alter them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preserve original transliteration and spelling conventions
rubrics_metrics.description: Just a word more on the subject of my spelling--in a transcript from the Greek and there exclusively--Greek names and places precisely as does the Greek author. I began this practice ... there has been till lately much astonishment at os and us, ai and oi, representing the same letters in Greek. Of a sudden, however, whether in translation or out of it, everybody seems committing the offence, although the adoption of u for v still presents such difficulty that it is a wonder how we have hitherto escaped 'Eyripides.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When transliterating Greek names and places, keep the forms the Greek author uses (preserve os/us, ai/oi distinctions, etc.). Be consistent and conservative in orthography rather than adopting fashionable or 'modernized' renderings.
